events.title: Lascaux Cave Paintings
events.blurb: In a limestone complex in southwestern France, Paleolithic artists over multiple generations painted some 6,000 bulls, deer, horses, and abstract signs along narrow corridors and a soaring "Hall of the Bulls" as large as a Romanesque nave. The largest painted bull is over five metres long. The cave was rediscovered in 1940 by four teenagers and their dog investigating a tree that had been uprooted by a storm.
events.revealBlurb: c. 17,000 BCE — Montignac, Dordogne. The original cave was closed to visitors in 1963 when tourist breath and carbon dioxide began damaging the pigments. Lascaux II, III, and IV — increasingly faithful replicas — have been opened to the public.

events.title: Tutankhamun Death Mask Created
events.blurb: Egyptian craftsmen fashioned a 10.2-kilogram gold funerary mask inlaid with lapis lazuli, carnelian, obsidian, and coloured glass to cover the mummy of a teenage pharaoh who had died at 18. The mask was sealed in a tomb packed with over 5,000 objects. The boy-king had been a minor figure; the tomb escaped the looting that emptied nearly every other Egyptian royal burial. It was untouched for 3,245 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1323 BCE — Tutankhamun died. Howard Carter's team uncovered the tomb on November 4, 1922. The mask now spends most of its time in a Cairo museum case and has been on world tours twice. The beard fell off during cleaning in 2014 and was hastily reattached with epoxy.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: David's Oath of the Horatii
events.blurb: A 36-year-old French painter, working in Rome, exhibited at the Paris Salon a sharply geometric, classically themed canvas of three Roman brothers swearing on their father's outstretched swords to fight for their city. Women wept in the shadows on the right. The painting's stark rejection of Rococo decoration and its austere civic virtue appealed exactly to the mood of a country five years from revolution.
events.revealBlurb: 1784 — Jacques-Louis David, exhibited at the Salon of 1785. Painted in Rome; shipped to Paris. David would become the leading painter of the French Revolution, personally designing the Tennis Court Oath as a commemorative picture and painting Marat dead in his bath.

events.title: Pollock's Drip Paintings
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American painter, working in a converted barn studio on Long Island, laid large unstretched canvases on the floor and moved around their edges pouring and flinging paint from sticks and hardened brushes. The resulting "drip paintings" rejected representational composition entirely in favour of overall visual rhythm. A 1949 Life magazine spread asked: "Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?" and made him instantly famous and nearly famously alcoholic.
events.revealBlurb: 1947 — Jackson Pollock began the drip technique in Springs, NY. He died in a car crash driving drunk on August 11, 1956, aged 44. His "No. 5, 1948" sold privately in 2006 for $140 million, briefly the highest price ever paid for a painting.

events.title: Invasion of Poland
events.blurb: At 4:43 in the morning a warship opened fire on a peninsula garrison, and within minutes armoured columns and aircraft were crossing a national border along a 1,600-kilometre front from three directions simultaneously. Two days later, two of the invader's neighbours declared war — and the world's largest conflict had begun.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1939 — the battleship Schleswig-Holstein fired the first shots at Westerplatte. The 88-man garrison held out for seven days against a force many times its size. Poland was split between Germany and the Soviet Union by October 6; a government-in-exile continued the fight from London.

events.title: Atlantic Charter
events.blurb: The leader of a neutral superpower and the leader of a beleaguered island nation met secretly aboard warships anchored off a foggy Newfoundland coast and jointly published a declaration of eight principles for the postwar world — including self-determination for peoples, freedom of the seas, and disarmament of aggressor nations — without committing either country to fight.
events.revealBlurb: August 14, 1941 — FDR and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter from HMS Prince of Wales and USS Augusta in Placentia Bay. The US was still technically neutral. The document became the founding framework for the United Nations. Churchill later noted that when the two men sang "O God Our Help in Ages Past" on deck, he felt the war was won.

events.title: Battle of the Coral Sea
events.blurb: Two opposing fleets manoeuvred for days without either side's surface ships ever sighting the other, their aircraft flying hundreds of miles over open ocean to find and strike carriers whose decks they could not see. One navy lost a fleet carrier and the other lost a light carrier — but the strategic consequence was that an invasion convoy turned back.
events.revealBlurb: May 4–8, 1942 — the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft. Neither fleet's ships came within sight of the other. Japan lost the light carrier Shōhō; the US lost USS Lexington. The two Japanese fleet carriers damaged at Coral Sea were then unavailable at Midway — a fact that proved decisive a month later.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Japan's Formal Surrender
events.blurb: Aboard a battleship anchored in a bay surrounded by an Allied fleet of 250 ships, representatives of a defeated empire signed the instrument of its unconditional surrender on a folding table set up on the deck, ending the largest armed conflict in human history after six years of fighting across every ocean and every inhabited continent.
events.revealBlurb: September 2, 1945 — USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. General MacArthur opened the ceremony: "We are gathered here to conclude a solemn agreement." The signing took 23 minutes. Japan's foreign minister, in top hat and tails, signed on behalf of the government. Allied Commander MacArthur used five pens to sign, giving them to survivors of Bataan, Corregidor, and others.

events.title: eBay Founded
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Iranian-American software engineer set up an online auction site over the Labor Day weekend, initially as a hobby project on a personal server. One of the first items sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to check whether he understood it was broken, the buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. The founder realized he had a business on his hands.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1995 — Pierre Omidyar. He originally named it AuctionWeb; renamed eBay in 1997, short for Echo Bay Technology, his consulting firm. The first commission was sent as a personal check for $241.19.

events.title: Hotmail Launched
events.blurb: Two engineers launched the world's first free web-based email service, deliberately choosing the launch date to coincide with a major American holiday celebrating independence. Users for the first time could access their email from any computer with a browser, independent of any particular ISP or employer. The service picked up a million users in six months.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1996 — Sabeer Bhatia and Jack Smith. They chose Independence Day to symbolize freedom from ISP lock-in. Microsoft acquired the service for $400 million 18 months later; it evolved into Outlook.com.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Facebook Buys WhatsApp
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley social-networking giant announced an agreement to acquire a five-year-old messaging app with 450 million users for $19 billion in cash and stock — the largest venture-backed acquisition in tech history. The app had 55 employees; one of its two founders had been rejected when he applied for a job at Facebook eight years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 2014 — Facebook buys WhatsApp; co-founders Jan Koum and Brian Acton. The service had been run on the principle of no ads, no gimmicks; Acton later left Facebook over disagreements about monetization and funded the rival Signal.

events.title: Pokémon Go Released
events.blurb: A free mobile game combining augmented reality with a beloved monster-catching franchise launched initially in Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Within a week, 21 million daily active users were wandering streets and parks staring at their phones, discovering virtual creatures superimposed on physical landmarks. It became the fastest mobile game to reach $500 million in revenue and, more strikingly, got millions of sedentary users to walk outside.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Niantic Inc. Within weeks, fatal accidents, trespassing incidents, and a small bump in physical activity had all been documented. The Pokémon Go wedding, held in New York's Central Park, was among the odder cultural moments of mid-2016.

events.title: First Ancient Olympic Games
events.blurb: A religious festival held every four years in honour of Zeus at a sacred grove in the western Peloponnese began with a single footrace — a sprint of about 192 metres — won by a cook from the nearby city of Elis. Over subsequent centuries, the games expanded to include additional running events, wrestling, boxing, pankration, pentathlon, and chariot racing. The festival ran continuously for nearly 1,200 years before a Christian emperor banned it.
events.revealBlurb: 776 BCE — traditional date of first games at Olympia; winner Coroebus of Elis. The festival was abolished by Emperor Theodosius I in 393 CE as part of his suppression of pagan rites. It was revived as the modern Olympics in Athens, 1896.

events.title: First Tour de France
events.blurb: A French sports newspaper, in an effort to increase circulation, organized a 2,428-kilometre bicycle race around the perimeter of France — six stages, each the length of an ultra-endurance event today, with sleep-deprived cyclists riding through the night on dirt roads with a single fixed gear. Sixty cyclists started; only 21 finished. A chimney sweep named Maurice Garin won the inaugural race over 19 days of riding.
events.revealBlurb: July 1-19, 1903 — organized by L'Auto magazine, a forerunner of L'Équipe. Garin's margin of victory was an implausible 2 hours 49 minutes. He was later stripped of his 1904 title for cheating (taking trains). The race continues annually with a couple of wartime interruptions.

events.title: Mark Spitz Wins Seventh Munich Gold
events.blurb: An American swimmer won his seventh gold medal of the Munich Games by anchoring the 4×100-metre medley relay team, setting a world record in every individual event he entered. No athlete had ever won more gold medals at a single Olympic Games, and he set or broke a world record in each of his seven finals.

events.title: Munich Olympics Massacre
events.blurb: Eight armed members of a Palestinian militant group scaled the perimeter fence of an Olympic Village at a German Summer Games, broke into the Israeli team's dormitory apartments, killed two Israeli athletes on the spot, and took nine others hostage. An inept German rescue operation at the military airfield where the hostages and captors had been flown ended with all nine hostages dead along with five of the eight attackers and one German police officer. The Games were suspended for a day, then resumed; the IOC president said that "the Games must go on."
events.revealBlurb: September 5-6, 1972 — Black September. IOC president: Avery Brundage. Israel's government launched a covert years-long assassination campaign against the attack's planners, known as Operation Wrath of God and dramatized in Spielberg's Munich (2005).

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: First Woman in Space
events.blurb: Valentina Tereshkova, a 26-year-old former textile factory worker and amateur parachutist with no pilot training, launched aboard Vostok 6 and orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days — more total time in space than all US astronauts who had flown to that date combined. She performed observations and photographed aerosol layers in Earth's atmosphere before parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Tereshkova selected herself from 400 applicants by writing a letter directly to the Soviet Space Program. She reportedly got motion sick and did not conduct some planned manual maneuvers, a fact kept classified for years. No woman flew in space again for 19 years. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: Voyager 1 Launch
events.blurb: NASA launched Voyager 1 on a trajectory exploiting a once-in-176-year alignment of the outer planets, allowing a single spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn using gravitational slingshots. The probe carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing sounds, music, and images representing life on Earth, selected by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan.
events.revealBlurb: September 5, 1977 — Voyager 1. It launched 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2, yet arrived at Jupiter first due to a faster trajectory. In 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. As of 2024 it is more than 24 billion km from Earth — so far that its radio signals, traveling at light speed, take over 22 hours to arrive.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: Kanye Interrupts Taylor Swift
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Chicago rapper walked onstage at a New York awards show as a 19-year-old country-pop singer was beginning her acceptance speech for Best Female Video, took the microphone from her, and declared that another nominee deserved to win. The interruption shocked the audience; the singer stood silently holding the award. It seeded a long-running and increasingly baroque public rivalry between the two performers that would include her several songs about him, his 2016 song about her, and a leaked phone call.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2009 — Kanye West interrupting Taylor Swift at the MTV VMAs. The other nominee Kanye was championing: Beyoncé. Beyoncé won the night's top award and gave her acceptance time back to Swift. The moment has replayed in the Swift-West feud for over 15 years.

events.title: Kim Kardashian "Breaks the Internet"
events.blurb: A 34-year-old reality TV star and entrepreneur appeared on the cover of a magazine nude, balancing a champagne glass on her bared posterior, with a headline directly daring the internet to be broken by it. The cover image was shared widely enough that the magazine's website crashed for short periods. The photograph — shot by a French photographer who had staged similar images four decades earlier — launched weeks of commentary about sexuality, race, body image, and the limits of viral marketing.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 2014 — Kim Kardashian on Paper magazine. Photographer Jean-Paul Goude had shot nearly identical images with other models in the 1970s and 80s, drawing accusations that he specifically emphasized and sexualized Black bodies. The cover did, in fact, briefly break the magazine's website.

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: Hamilton Opens on Broadway
events.blurb: A hip-hop-based musical about the founding-era American politician Alexander Hamilton, written by a 35-year-old playwright-composer who had performed an early version at a White House poetry event in 2009, opened on Broadway after a sold-out off-Broadway run. The show's casting of non-white actors as the Founding Fathers, its rapid-fire rap-through-historical-politics, and its grand storytelling about ambition and legacy made it a generational phenomenon. Tickets sold on the secondary market for over $1,000.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 2015 — Lin-Manuel Miranda as Hamilton at the Richard Rodgers Theatre. The show won 11 Tony Awards in 2016 and a Pulitzer Prize for Drama. A professionally filmed version premiered on Disney+ on July 3, 2020 during the COVID pandemic, drawing enormous viewership.

events.title: Raja Harishchandra Released
events.blurb: A mythological silent film about the legendarily truthful king Harishchandra — shot in Bombay using an all-male cast because no actress would agree to appear on screen — opened at the Coronation Cinematograph in Girgaon and became India's first feature film, running 3,700 feet of hand-cranked footage. Its creator had spent over a year learning to develop film himself after being refused laboratory access.
events.revealBlurb: May 3, 1913 — Dadasaheb Phalke's debut. He was a printer by trade. Legend says he watched The Life of Christ (1906) in Bombay and decided India needed its own screen mythology. All the female roles were played by male wrestlers and cooks; no respectable woman would work in pictures.

events.title: Film and Television Institute of India Founded
events.blurb: A national school for cinema craft, established on the former premises of a shuttered studio whose golden era had passed, began training directors, cinematographers, and sound engineers in a new medium that independent India wanted to shape on its own terms. Its graduates would go on to redefine the aesthetic vocabulary of both art-house and popular Indian filmmaking.
events.revealBlurb: 1960, Pune. Built inside the Prabhat Film Company compound. Satyajit Ray advised on its curriculum. Early graduates include Shyam Benegal, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Mrinal Sen, Girish Karnad — essentially the entire generation that invented Indian parallel cinema.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: "Naatu Naatu" Wins Academy Award
events.blurb: A Telugu period action film about two real freedom fighters reimagined as friends on opposite sides of a colonial conflict produced a seven-minute dance sequence that, when performed live at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, brought an Oscars audience to its feet. The song became the first from an Indian film to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 2023 — the 95th Academy Awards. Composer M.M. Keeravani and lyricist Chandrabose won. Director S.S. Rajamouli's RRR had not been submitted as India's official Oscar entry — it qualified independently through its US distributor. Singers Rahul Sipligunj and Kaala Bhairava performed barefoot on the Oscars stage.

events.title: Jawan Released
events.blurb: A Tamil director's Hindi-film debut — a dual-role action thriller mixing vigilante politics with hospital corruption — earned ₹75 crore on its opening day, making it the highest-opening-day gross in Hindi cinema at the time, then crossed ₹600 crore domestically, becoming the first Hindi film to do so. Its release capped a year in which its star reclaimed the top of the industry after a decade's absence.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 2023 — directed by Atlee. Shah Rukh Khan's return, following Pathaan earlier that year, made 2023 the most commercially dominant single-year performance by any one actor in Bollywood history. The film's opening credits featured cameos by over thirty prominent South Indian actors.

events.title: Integrated Circuit Demonstrated
events.blurb: An engineer at a Dallas electronics company demonstrated a germanium chip the size of a paperclip with a working oscillator etched directly onto its surface — the first integrated circuit, combining multiple transistors, resistors, and capacitors into a single monolithic piece of semiconductor. The invention would shrink electronic components by orders of magnitude every decade for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 1958 — Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments. Robert Noyce at Fairchild developed a similar design independently a few months later using silicon; his is the variant the industry actually used. Kilby won the 2000 Nobel; Noyce had died in 1990 and so was ineligible.

events.title: First Cellular Phone Call
events.blurb: A Motorola engineer, standing on a Manhattan street with a 1.1-kilogram "brick" prototype handset to his ear, placed a phone call to his chief rival at a competing company's research lab — and made sure to inform him what he was doing. The handset's battery gave 35 minutes of talk time after 10 hours of charging. Motorola would spend another decade getting a lighter version to market.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1973 — Martin Cooper of Motorola called Joel Engel at Bell Labs. The prototype was the DynaTAC 8000x. It sold commercially in 1983 for $3,995. Cooper later said he'd been inspired by the communicator in Star Trek.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: Tesla Model S Released
events.blurb: A California electric-vehicle startup, founded a decade earlier and funded partly by the same entrepreneur who had sold PayPal, delivered the first units of a four-door luxury sedan with a fully electric drivetrain, over-the-air software updates, a 17-inch touchscreen, and a 500-kilometre range. Legacy automakers had considered electric cars a niche; the Model S made them convincingly better than gasoline vehicles in several important dimensions.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 2012 — Tesla Model S, led by Elon Musk. Motor Trend named it Car of the Year. The "Ludicrous Mode" software option made it accelerate 0-60 mph in under 3 seconds. Tesla passed $1 trillion valuation in 2021, briefly the first automaker to do so.

events.title: Atari 2600 Launches
events.blurb: For the first time, a home console used interchangeable cartridges — meaning the same hardware could play a new game every week. Atari sold 250,000 units in the first months at $199 apiece. Within three years the living room had replaced the arcade as the primary venue for video games.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 1977 — Atari released the Video Computer System (renamed 2600 in 1982). By 1982, 15 million 2600s had been sold and the console was generating $2 billion in annual revenue.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Sonic the Hedgehog Released for Sega Genesis
events.blurb: Sega needed a mascot to fight Mario. The result was a blue hedgehog who could run faster than the screen could scroll, built around a physics engine that turned speed itself into the core gameplay mechanic. It shipped bundled with the Genesis in North America, helped Sega capture 65 percent of the console market.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1991 — Sonic the Hedgehog launched in North America for the Sega Genesis. Sega's North American market share climbed from 15% to 65% during the game's first year. The Sonic franchise has since sold over 1.5 billion games.

events.title: Oculus Rift Kickstarter Campaign Launches
events.blurb: A 19-year-old in his parents' garage had spent years building virtual reality headsets from scavenged parts. His Kickstarter campaign asked for $250,000 to build a developer kit. It raised $2.4 million from nearly 10,000 backers. Two years later, Facebook acquired his company for $2 billion.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 2012 — Palmer Luckey launched the Oculus Rift Kickstarter, raising 974% of its $250,000 goal. Facebook (now Meta) acquired Oculus VR in March 2014 for approximately $2 billion.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: University of Bologna Founded
events.blurb: A self-organized guild of foreign students in a northern Italian city hired local scholars to lecture them on civil and canon law, and the informal arrangement crystallized into something new: a chartered community with legal privileges, standardized exams, and a governing rector elected by the students themselves. It is considered the oldest continuously operating university in the Western world.
events.revealBlurb: 1088 — date traditionally given, though the institution evolved over decades. The students were mostly the sons of wealthy families across Europe; they often hired the professors directly and fined them for being late to class. Petrarch, Dante, Copernicus, and Erasmus all studied there.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Bacon's Rebellion Burns Jamestown
events.blurb: A Virginia planter named Nathaniel Bacon rallied a mixed force of frontier settlers, indentured servants, and enslaved Africans against the colonial governor and marched on the capital, burning Jamestown to the ground. The uprising — the largest armed revolt in colonial America before the Revolution — exposed deep class and racial tensions that led planters to harden the legal distinction between Black slaves and white laborers.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1676 — Jamestown, Virginia. Bacon died of dysentery six weeks after burning the capital, ending the rebellion without a battle. Historians argue his multiracial army scared Virginia's elite so badly they accelerated the shift to race-based chattel slavery.

events.title: Teapot Dome: Senate Investigation Opens
events.blurb: The Senate launched its first formal investigation into the Teapot Dome oil fields that autumn, following revelations that Interior Secretary Albert Fall had secretly leased federal naval petroleum reserves in Wyoming and California to private oil companies in exchange for personal cash loans and gifts totaling roughly $400,000. Fall would become the first U.S. Cabinet member ever convicted of a crime committed while in office.
events.revealBlurb: October 1923 — Washington, D.C. The oil companies that paid the bribes — Sinclair Oil and Pan American Petroleum — were acquitted at trial; only the man who took the bribes was convicted. President Harding died of a heart attack in August 1923, before the scandal fully broke.

events.title: Nixon Resigns the Presidency
events.blurb: That evening, Richard Nixon became the first and only U.S. president to resign from office, delivering a nationally televised address from the Oval Office in which he announced his departure would take effect at noon the following day. The resignation came after the release of the "smoking gun" tape proved Nixon had personally directed the Watergate cover-up six days after the break-in, making his impeachment and Senate conviction certain.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1974 — The Oval Office. Nixon's approval rating the week of his resignation was 24%. Gerald Ford pardoned him one month later, saying "our long national nightmare is over" — a pardon that likely cost Ford the 1976 election. Nixon is the only president ever to resign.

events.title: September 11 Terrorist Attacks
events.blurb: That morning, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers commandeered four commercial aircraft and flew two into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon, and a fourth — whose passengers revolted and forced the plane down — into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the United States' longest wars, a sweeping reorganization of domestic security, and a generation of political consequence.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — New York, Virginia, Pennsylvania. The North Tower stood 102 minutes after impact; the South Tower collapsed first, 56 minutes after being hit, because the plane struck lower floors. The 9/11 Commission found no credible evidence of state sponsorship by any foreign government.

events.title: Lehman Brothers Collapses: 2008 Financial Crisis
events.blurb: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy — the largest bankruptcy in American history, with over $600 billion in assets — triggering a global financial panic that erased more than $10 trillion in U.S. household wealth and produced the worst economic downturn since the 1930s. The failure stemmed from the firm's enormous exposure to mortgage-backed securities tied to a collapsing housing market.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 2008 — New York City. The Federal Reserve and Treasury had just rescued Bear Stearns and Fannie Mae but declined to backstop Lehman. The Dow dropped 504 points that day — and lost another 33% over the next three months. TARP, a $700 billion bank rescue program, was signed into law 19 days later.

events.title: Battle of Marathon
events.blurb: A force of 10,000 Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeated a Persian expedition of 25,000 troops and cavalry on a coastal plain 40 kilometres northeast of Athens. The Athenian commander had tricked the Persians into overextending on the wings, then enveloped them. The Greek victory preserved Athenian independence against the greatest military empire of the age and, by extension, the classical Greek cultural project. A runner dispatched to Athens with news of the victory is said to have expired on arrival.
events.revealBlurb: c. September 12, 490 BCE. Commander: Miltiades. The runner Pheidippides is the foundation myth of the marathon road race; the distance — 42.195 km — matches the run from the battlefield to Athens only coincidentally, set for the 1908 London Olympics.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.blurb: A Greek allied fleet of roughly 370 triremes, lured into position by a false message from the Athenian commander, engaged a Persian fleet of perhaps 800 in the narrow straits between a small island and the Athenian mainland coast. The Persian ships, crowded in the strait, could not maneuver; the Greek triremes rammed them methodically for twelve hours. Over 200 Persian ships were sunk or captured. The Persian king watched the disaster unfold from a throne on the adjacent mainland.
events.revealBlurb: September 480 BCE — Themistocles, Athenian strategos. The Persian king was Xerxes I; he retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving a smaller force that was destroyed at Plataea the following year. Aeschylus, who had fought at Salamis himself, wrote a play about it eight years later.

events.title: Battle of Chaeronea
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's army of 32,000 defeated a combined Athenian-Theban force of similar size in central Greece, ending the independence of the classical Greek city-states. The victor's 18-year-old son, commanding the Macedonian left wing, personally broke the famous Sacred Band of Thebes — a unit of 300 elite warrior-lovers who died to the man. The defeat of the city-states unified Greece under Macedonian hegemony and set up the Asian conquests that would follow.
events.revealBlurb: August 338 BCE — King Philip II and his son Alexander. The Sacred Band of Thebes had won every battle it had fought for 40 years; it lost only at Chaeronea. Philip erected a stone lion over their mass grave; the lion, damaged over millennia, was restored in 1902 and still stands there.

events.title: Battle of Gaugamela
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's force of 47,000 defeated a Persian imperial army of perhaps 250,000 in the open plains of a Mesopotamian valley. The Macedonian king personally led the decisive cavalry charge at a gap that opened in the Persian centre when its king's bodyguards shifted to counter a feint on the wings. The Persian king fled the field, abandoning his empire; he was murdered by his own satraps a year later. Alexander entered Babylon as the new lord of Asia.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 331 BCE — Alexander III of Macedon vs. Darius III of Persia. Alexander had refused his general Parmenion's advice to attack at night; he reportedly said "I will not steal my victory." Darius fled to Bactria, where he was killed by his cousin Bessus — who was then captured and executed by Alexander.

events.title: Crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth
events.blurb: A Jewish teacher from a Galilean town, who had spent a few years preaching an apocalyptic ethical message and gathering followers, was arrested by Temple authorities in the Judean capital during a Passover festival, handed to the Roman prefect, and crucified on a charge of claiming to be "King of the Jews." He was 33. A small community of his followers, convinced he had risen from the dead three days later, carried his teachings out of Judea; within three centuries their movement was the state religion of the Roman Empire.
events.revealBlurb: c. April 3, 33 CE — Jesus of Nazareth; prefect Pontius Pilate. The precise date is debated; April 7, 30 CE is an alternative. Christianity spread slowly across the first three centuries; Emperor Constantine's 313 CE Edict of Milan ended persecution; Theodosius I made it the official Roman religion in 380 CE.

events.title: Oprah's "You Get a Car!"
events.blurb: An American daytime talk-show host opened her show's 19th-season premiere by giving a brand-new compact sedan to each of 276 audience members who, she said, had been nominated by loved ones as desperately needing a new vehicle. She turned to a different audience section and shouted: "You get a car! You get a car!" each audience member in turn. The sustained joy — and the full-volume shouting — became a lasting cultural moment captured in countless memes and parodies.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2004 — Oprah Winfrey on The Oprah Winfrey Show. The cars were Pontiac G6 sedans donated by General Motors, which covered the ~$7 million cost as a promotion. Audience members were reportedly shocked to discover the IRS expected them to pay tax on the "gift" of around $7,000.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Obama Inaugurated
events.blurb: A 47-year-old former U.S. Senator from Illinois, the son of a Kenyan father and a Kansas mother, was sworn in as the 44th President of the United States on a cold winter morning at the U.S. Capitol. Some 1.8 million people watched from the National Mall — the largest crowd ever gathered in the capital for any purpose. Chief Justice John Roberts flubbed the oath of office so badly that they re-did it privately the following day out of constitutional caution.
events.revealBlurb: January 20, 2009 — Barack Obama. Aretha Franklin's performance of "My Country, 'Tis of Thee" in a famously enormous bow-tied hat became an iconic image. Michelle Obama wore a lemongrass-yellow Isabel Toledo ensemble; she later said it came from a "just make the best of this" impulse.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Lady Gaga's Meat Dress
events.blurb: A 24-year-old American pop singer arrived at a New York awards show wearing an outfit made from 50 pounds of raw Argentine beef — flank steak fashioned into a sleeveless dress, a matching hat, a handbag, and shoes. She told a late-night host the ensemble was a protest against a military policy excluding openly gay service members. PETA criticized it; steak prices nationwide did not apparently change. The dress was later preserved as beef jerky and displayed at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 2010 — Lady Gaga (Stefani Germanotta) at the MTV VMAs. Designer Franc Fernandez. The dress won her five VMAs that night, including Video of the Year for "Bad Romance." It is now permanently on display in Cleveland.

events.title: Virgil's Aeneid
events.blurb: A 51-year-old Roman poet died with his commissioned national epic not quite finished, asking on his deathbed that the unfinished manuscript be burned. The emperor he had spent a decade writing it for overruled him. The twelve-book poem traced the mythical origins of Rome to a Trojan prince fleeing the burning city. It became, and remains, the canonical literary masterpiece of Latin civilization.
events.revealBlurb: 19 BCE — Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro). Emperor Augustus saved the text. Virgil's funeral procession was attended by the emperor himself. Dante took Virgil as his guide through Hell and Purgatory in The Divine Comedy; Milton modeled Paradise Lost on the Aeneid.

events.title: Dante Completes Divine Comedy
events.blurb: A 56-year-old exiled Florentine poet completed the third and final part of a long allegorical poem describing his journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, guided by a Roman poet and his earthly beloved. Written in Italian rather than Latin, it pulled the vernacular into literary respectability. He died within months of finishing.
events.revealBlurb: 1320 — Dante Alighieri. He had been exiled from Florence in 1302 over factional politics; he never returned. The last 13 cantos of Paradiso were missing for months after his death until his son Jacopo found them in a secret cavity in a wall, supposedly after Dante appeared in a dream.

events.title: Machiavelli Writes The Prince
events.blurb: An unemployed former Florentine civil servant, exiled from the city after a change of regime, wrote a compact political treatise in the form of advice to a hereditary ruler on how to acquire and maintain power. Its flat, unsentimental analysis of the uses of cruelty, deception, and popular love versus fear shocked readers and made its author's name a by-word for cynical politics. It remained unpublished until five years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: 1513 — Niccolò Machiavelli. The treatise was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, who almost certainly never read it. Published 1532 and promptly placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Still in print 500 years later.

events.title: Walden Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Massachusetts essayist, graduate of Harvard, former schoolteacher, and occasional pencil-factory worker, published an account of two years and two months he had spent living in a cabin he had built himself beside a glacier-pond near Concord. The book mixed natural observation, economic criticism, and philosophical reflection. It sold slowly; its reputation grew after the author's early death seven years later, and he is now considered one of the founders of American nature writing.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1854 — Henry David Thoreau. He had lived at Walden Pond 1845-47. The pond was, contrary to legend, a short walk from his family home; his mother did his laundry. Thoreau's civil-disobedience essay would later inspire Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: Liverpool-Manchester Railway Opens
events.blurb: The world's first inter-city passenger railway line opened with ceremony, carrying dignitaries including the Duke of Wellington on eight parallel trains along a 56-kilometre line linking the port of Liverpool with the cotton-manufacturing centre of Manchester. A parliamentary member, William Huskisson, stepped onto the tracks at a refueling stop and was struck by an oncoming locomotive. He died that evening — the first well-known railway fatality.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1830 — designed by George Stephenson. Huskisson is universally regarded as the first prominent casualty of the railway age, though he was not strictly the first railway death. The line ran horse- and steam-hauled freight alongside passengers for its first decades.

events.title: Bessemer Steel Process
events.blurb: A 42-year-old English inventor read a paper to a scientific conference describing a new way to turn pig iron into steel by blowing air through molten metal in a pear-shaped converter. The oxidation removed carbon impurities in minutes rather than the hours required by existing methods, and without extra fuel. The process cut steel prices by 80 percent. Within a generation, steel displaced iron in railways, ships, and skyscrapers.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1856 — Henry Bessemer at the British Association meeting in Cheltenham. He was knighted in 1879. American steelmakers led by Andrew Carnegie built the largest Bessemer operations in the world around Pittsburgh.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Mozart's Requiem Unfinished
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Austrian composer who had been commissioned by a mysterious stranger six months earlier to compose a requiem Mass for an anonymous client died in his Vienna apartment with the work unfinished. Much of the "Dies irae" and "Lacrimosa" had been sketched only. His widow, in desperate financial circumstances, had a student complete the work to secure the remaining half of the commission fee.
events.revealBlurb: December 5, 1791 — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, aged 35. The mysterious stranger was Count Walsegg, who meant to pass the work off as his own for his late wife. Mozart's student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it; his contributions have been debated ever since.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: Beatles on Ed Sullivan
events.blurb: Four young British musicians from a northwestern English port city performed live on a Sunday-evening American variety show before an audience of 73 million viewers — at the time the largest in U.S. television history. The hysteria had preceded them: 7,000 people had mobbed their arrival at a New York airport two days earlier. Adult commentators dismissed them as a passing fad; younger Americans rearranged their evening to watch.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1964 — The Beatles at Studio 50, Manhattan. The crime rate during the broadcast was unusually low — even, it was said, in Times Square. They returned the next two Sundays for back-to-back appearances.

events.title: Monterey Pop Festival
events.blurb: A three-day rock festival on a California coastal fairground — the first major rock festival of the decade and the template for what came later — introduced American audiences to a left-handed guitarist recently returned from London, a young Otis Redding, and Janis Joplin. The left-hander, during his set, laid his guitar on the stage, knelt over it, and set it on fire with lighter fluid. The audience had not imagined such a thing was possible.
events.revealBlurb: June 16-18, 1967 — the guitarist was Jimi Hendrix, on the closing Sunday. Monterey Pop Festival drew 200,000 people. The Mamas & the Papas had organized it; proceeds went to charity. Paul McCartney recommended Hendrix and The Who to the organizers.

events.title: Rapper's Delight Released
events.blurb: Three rappers from the New York metro area, assembled by an independent label, released a 15-minute track over a bassline lifted from a recent disco hit. It was the first hip-hop single to reach the U.S. Billboard Top 40. The culture it came from had been thriving in parks and clubs around the Bronx for six years; this record introduced it to mainstream white America and set rap on the path from subcultural movement to dominant global genre.
events.revealBlurb: September 1979 — Sugarhill Gang on Sugar Hill Records. The bassline was from Chic's "Good Times"; Chic's Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards sued and received co-writing credit. The track went platinum in the US and hit #3 in the UK.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green Released in Japan
events.blurb: A game about capturing and training pocket monsters on a handheld with a dying link cable had been in development for six years and nearly bankrupted its studio twice. It released quietly on a console most retailers considered obsolete. Within months it had detonated into the fastest-growing entertainment franchise in Japanese history.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1996 — Pokémon Red and Green launched for Game Boy in Japan. By the end of 1996 they had sold 3.6 million copies in Japan alone; the franchise has since generated over $150 billion, making it the highest-grossing media franchise in history.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Grand Theft Auto V Released
events.blurb: A crime game set in a fictionalised Los Angeles earned $800 million on its first day and $1 billion within three days — the fastest any entertainment product in history had reached that figure at that time. Guinness certified six world records on launch day. More than a decade later it continues to generate revenue through its online component.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 2013 — GTA V launched for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It broke six Guinness World Records including fastest entertainment property to gross $1 billion. The game has sold over 200 million copies. GTA Online continues to generate over $1 billion annually.

events.title: Stonehenge Completed
events.blurb: Over the course of a millennium, Neolithic builders on a chalk plain in southern England erected a circular arrangement of massive standing stones — some weighing 25 tonnes, dragged from quarries over 250 kilometres away — fitted together with mortise-and-tenon joints as if they were timber. The monument aligns with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Its precise purpose — ritual, astronomical, funerary — has been debated for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2000 BCE — main sarsen-circle completion on Salisbury Plain. The smaller "bluestones," of volcanic rock, came from the Preseli Hills in Wales. Construction had begun about 5,000 years ago in earthen-bank form. The monument predates the druids by 2,000 years, despite the misattribution.

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Sagrada Família Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a Catholic basilica in the Catalan capital, funded by donations alone — a condition that would stretch the project across a century and a half. The original architect was replaced after one year by a 31-year-old ferociously religious designer who would pour the rest of his life into the project, combining Gothic and Art Nouveau influences into a style of his own. He would die 43 years later, hit by a tram on the street outside; only a fraction of the church was finished. Construction continues today.
events.revealBlurb: March 19, 1882 — original architect Francisco de Paula del Villar; succeeded 1883 by Antoni Gaudí. Gaudí devoted the last 15 years of his life exclusively to the project. He was hit by a tram on June 7, 1926; his grave is in the crypt. Completion is projected for 2026 — a century after his death.

events.title: Statue of Liberty Dedicated
events.blurb: A 46-metre-tall copper statue of a robed woman holding a torch, a gift from the French people commemorating American independence (with an eye toward French republican aspirations), was dedicated on a small island in New York Harbor in the rain. It had been designed by a French sculptor, its internal iron framework engineered by the man who would five years later design a certain Paris tower, and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 1886 — sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi; engineer Gustave Eiffel. The statue was meant to arrive for the 1876 centennial; it missed by a decade due to fundraising troubles. The poem on its pedestal ("Give me your tired, your poor...") was added in 1903 from a sonnet by Emma Lazarus.

events.title: Channel Tunnel Opens
events.blurb: A 50-kilometre twin-bore railway tunnel under the English Channel opened, linking France to Britain below the sea floor for the first time in 8,000 years. The tunnel had been proposed repeatedly since the early 19th century but had always been shelved on defensive grounds; the end of the Cold War and European integration finally made it buildable. Construction had involved eleven tunnel-boring machines drilling simultaneously from both sides; the breakthrough was within 35 centimetres alignment.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1994 — Queen Elizabeth II and President François Mitterrand cut a ribbon jointly. Total project cost: £9 billion, roughly 80 percent over budget. The tunnel is used by Eurostar passenger trains and the freight-carrying Shuttle. Trains reach 160 km/h underground.

events.title: New Zealand Grants Women's Suffrage
events.blurb: The governor of a British colony in the South Pacific gave royal assent to an electoral act adding "and women" to the existing definition of qualified voters, making the colony the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the national franchise. Roughly 90,000 women registered within weeks; 82 percent of them turned out for the first subsequent election.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1893 — campaigners including Kate Sheppard delivered a petition a quarter of a kilometre long with nearly 32,000 signatures. The date is now Suffrage Day in New Zealand. Sheppard appears on the country's ten-dollar note.

events.title: First Birth Control Clinic
events.blurb: A public-health nurse in a Brooklyn neighbourhood of Manhattan opened a storefront clinic that distributed contraceptive information, pamphlets, and pessaries to working-class women. She had fled to Europe the previous year to escape indictment under federal obscenity laws for writing about contraception; she now dared local authorities to close her. They obliged on day nine.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1916 — Margaret Sanger in Brownsville, Brooklyn. She was jailed for 30 days. Her appeal established that doctors could legally prescribe contraception. She founded what would become Planned Parenthood a decade later.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Disappears
events.blurb: On the penultimate leg of an around-the-world flight at the equator, a 39-year-old American aviator and her navigator took off from a Pacific airstrip bound for a tiny coral island 4,100 kilometres away. Her final radio messages reported low fuel and inability to locate the island. A Navy search of 400,000 square kilometres of ocean found nothing. Her disappearance has launched a hundred books and at least three feature films.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1937 — Earhart and Fred Noonan bound for Howland Island. Prevailing theories: ran out of fuel and ditched; landed on uninhabited Nikumaroro and died of thirst; captured by the Japanese. No conclusive physical evidence exists.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes
events.blurb: A 29-year-old women's tennis champion beat a 55-year-old former men's Wimbledon champion in straight sets at a televised exhibition match at a Houston indoor arena, before 30,000 spectators and an estimated 90 million television viewers worldwide. The older player had spent months mocking women's tennis in the press; he entered the arena on a rickshaw pulled by models in skimpy outfits and gave her a Sugar Daddy lollipop at the net.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1973 — Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 at the Houston Astrodome. King had threatened to boycott the US Open unless prize money was equal; Forest Hills agreed in time for the tournament that August — the first Slam to do so.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Magellan Sets Sail
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Portuguese-born captain, working for the Spanish crown because his own king had rejected his project, left a Sevillian port with five small ships and 270 men on a westward voyage to the spice-rich islands of Southeast Asia. He was convinced a sea passage through the Americas existed. He would find it — and a strait at the continent's southern tip is now named after him — but he would never see its other end.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1519 — Ferdinand Magellan. He was killed on the Philippine island of Mactan on April 27, 1521 by troops of the local chief Lapu-Lapu. One of his five ships completed the first circumnavigation — returning with 18 survivors and a load of cloves that covered the entire expedition's costs.

events.title: Henry VIII Breaks with Rome
events.blurb: An English parliament passed an Act of Supremacy declaring the king — who had wanted for years to annul his marriage to a Spanish princess who had given him no male heir, and whom the pope had refused — the "Supreme Head" of the Church of England. The break with Rome was not primarily theological; the king remained Catholic in doctrine for the rest of his life. It rewrote England's religious, political, and property landscape for the next century.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1534 — Henry VIII. He had already married Anne Boleyn (his second wife) in secret in January 1533. The archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, had annulled his first marriage in May. Henry would have six wives; two were beheaded, two divorced, one died in childbirth.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Haiti Declares Independence
events.blurb: A former slave turned general, addressing a small crowd at a town on a Caribbean island, declared the independence of a new sovereign state that replaced a French sugar colony. It took the name of the original Taíno indigenous word for the island. It was the first independent state in Latin America, the only one to emerge from a successful slave revolt, and the second republic in the Western hemisphere. European powers reacted with diplomatic ostracism; the United States refused recognition for 58 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1804 — Jean-Jacques Dessalines at Gonaïves, Haiti. France demanded reparations for "lost property" — 150 million francs — that Haiti finished paying only in 1947. The combination of debt, ostracism, and internal strife has shaped Haitian poverty for two centuries.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: Grito de Dolores
events.blurb: A 57-year-old Catholic priest in a rural Mexican town, learning that a conspiracy of criollo-elite revolutionaries had been uncovered, rang his church bell in the middle of the night to summon his parishioners and call for the overthrow of Spanish colonial rule. He led his ragged army of peasants and mestizos toward the capital; the colonial government crushed them within four months and he was shot. The rebellion he had started, though, continued for 11 more years.
events.revealBlurb: September 16, 1810 — Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla at Dolores, Guanajuato. The exact wording of his "grito" is not recorded. Hidalgo was captured in March 1811 and executed by firing squad on July 30, 1811. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day; the President still rings the bell each year.

events.title: Napoleon Invades Russia
events.blurb: A French emperor crossed the Neman River into Russian territory with the largest army Europe had ever seen — 680,000 men drawn from across his continental empire. His objectives were to compel Russia back into a trade embargo against Britain and to break Russian military power. The Russians fell back, burning as they withdrew, refusing pitched battle. The French reached Moscow in September to find it empty and soon burning. The retreat home through a catastrophic winter would destroy almost the entire army.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1812 — the Neman crossing. Of the 680,000 who crossed east, perhaps 40,000 returned. The retreat featured the famous crossing of the Berezina River, where improvised pontoon bridges collapsed under packed refugees; tens of thousands died in the icy water.

events.title: "Who Shot J.R.?" Revealed
events.blurb: An estimated 83 million American viewers — 76 percent of all active television sets at the time — tuned in to a prime-time U.S. soap opera to learn who had fired the cliffhanger-ending shot that had kept the nation guessing for eight months. At the time it was the most-watched single program in television history. Souvenir T-shirts, novelty songs, and betting pools had all sprouted during the summer hiatus between seasons.
