events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1980 — Dallas, episode "Who Done It." The shooter was Kristin Shepard, played by Mary Crosby. J.R. Ewing survived. The "Who Shot J.R.?" plot is considered a pioneer of the season-ending cliffhanger in prime-time television.

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer. The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: The Breakfast Club Released
events.blurb: A film about five high-school students from different cliques stuck together for a Saturday detention in the school library opened in American theatres. The cast — a nerd, a jock, a princess, a rebel, a weirdo — talked, argued, and bonded over 97 minutes in a script tight enough that one actor later claimed much of it felt improvised. The film defined a style of introspective teen comedy-drama the decade would become known for. It grossed $45 million on a $1 million budget.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1985 — John Hughes directing Emilio Estevez, Molly Ringwald, Judd Nelson, Ally Sheedy, and Anthony Michael Hall. Hughes had written the script in a single weekend, 1982. The final fist-pump shot, set to Simple Minds' "Don't You (Forget About Me)," became iconic.

events.title: Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from Aberdeen, Washington released their second album featuring a swimming infant reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. Within three months it had displaced a reigning pop star's record from the top of the Billboard 200, and its lead single's music video received more plays on music television than any previous video.

events.title: Friends Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour NBC sitcom about six young adults — a food chef, an aspiring actor, a paleontologist, a masseuse, a restaurant hostess, and a data processor — sharing two Greenwich Village apartments premiered to middling reviews and moderate ratings. The show would run ten years, cement the demographic of "twentysomething in Manhattan" as a comedy staple, and command an unprecedented $1 million per episode per cast member in its final season. Its title sequence featured six friends splashing in a fountain.
events.revealBlurb: September 22, 1994 — Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Lisa Kudrow, Matt LeBlanc, Matthew Perry, David Schwimmer. Created by Marta Kauffman and David Crane. The cast negotiated as a union, a strategy that pushed their salary to the stratosphere. Perry died in 2023 at 54.

events.title: Pythagorean Theorem Proven in Greek School
events.blurb: Greek mathematicians of the Pythagorean school produced the first known formal proof that in any right-angled triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two — a relationship that had been known empirically by Babylonian and Egyptian surveyors for over a thousand years, but never demonstrated to follow necessarily from first principles.
events.revealBlurb: c. 530 BCE — the theorem was known to Babylonian scribes by 1900 BCE, long before Pythagoras was born. What his school contributed was the idea of proving it. There are over 370 known distinct proofs; one appears in Euclid's Elements, another was submitted by a sitting U.S. President (James Garfield) to a mathematics journal in 1876.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Penicillin Discovered
events.blurb: Returning from vacation, a bacteriologist noticed a petri dish of Staphylococcus bacteria had been contaminated by a mold that had dissolved the surrounding bacterial colonies into clear halos. He cultured the mold — Penicillium notatum — and determined it produced a substance lethal to bacteria, naming it penicillin.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: Endosymbiotic Theory Published
events.blurb: A paper proposed that the energy-producing mitochondria and photosynthetic chloroplasts inside complex cells were originally free-living bacteria that had been engulfed by a host cell and retained over billions of years — a radical claim that the cell's most vital structures were once independent organisms. The paper had been rejected by approximately fifteen journals before finding a publisher.
events.revealBlurb: June 1967 — Lynn Margulis submitted the paper under her married surname Sagan; it became one of biology's most-cited papers after decades of derision. Her critics called it "too fantastic." When the hypothesis was tested by comparing DNA in mitochondria to bacterial DNA in the 1980s, it matched almost exactly.

events.title: First Jazz Recording
events.blurb: Five white musicians from New Orleans, working under the slightly misspelled name "Original Dixieland Jass Band," recorded two sides for a Victor label at a New York studio: "Livery Stable Blues" and "Dixie Jass Band One Step." The 78 sold a million copies, breaking sales records, and introduced the word "jazz" to most Americans. Black New Orleans musicians had been playing the style for years; the first commercial recording went to imitators.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 1917 — recorded in NYC; released March 7, 1917. The ODJB's cornetist Nick LaRocca later claimed, implausibly, to have invented jazz. The ethical irony of white performers first commercializing a Black art form was noted at the time and has only grown.

events.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
events.blurb: A 24-year-old cornetist who had grown up in the poorest section of New Orleans walked into a Chicago studio for the first session with a small band of his own. Over the next three years, the "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" sessions would reshape popular music. His vocal improvisation on "Heebie Jeebies" — a chorus of nonsense syllables when he claimed to drop his lyric sheet — launched scat singing. His trumpet solos made the individual improvisation the heart of jazz.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1925 — Louis Armstrong at OKeh Records, Chicago. The "Heebie Jeebies" vocal made him a national figure. He would become the first African-American to host a nationally sponsored radio show.

events.title: Bob Marley's Exodus Released
events.blurb: A Jamaican reggae star, recovering in a London flat after being shot in an assassination attempt at his home five months earlier, released his ninth studio album. Its tracks — "Three Little Birds," "One Love," "Jamming," "Waiting in Vain," and the title track — would become the core of his international legacy. Time magazine named it the album of the century. He had fled to London for his safety; the exile shaped the record.
events.revealBlurb: June 3, 1977 — Bob Marley and the Wailers. The album was recorded at Island Studios in London. The attempted assassination on December 3, 1976 had injured him, his wife, and his manager. Marley would die of cancer at 36 in 1981.

events.title: John Lennon Shot
events.blurb: A 40-year-old former Beatle, returning to his Manhattan apartment building with his wife after a late-night recording session, was shot four times in the back at close range by a young man he had signed an autograph for earlier that afternoon. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital 20 minutes later. Vigils were held around the world. His wife asked that his birthday be celebrated with international moments of silence, which has since become a yearly tradition.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1980 — John Lennon at The Dakota, NYC. Shooter Mark David Chapman remains in prison, denied parole 13 times. Lennon's album "Double Fantasy" had been released three weeks earlier; it took on enormous posthumous sales.

events.title: Nirvana's Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from the Pacific Northwest released their second album — recorded for $65,000, with a cover showing a naked infant underwater reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. The album's lead single had been written, according to the band, to sound "like the Pixies" and made a mockery of that idea. By January it had displaced Michael Jackson's "Dangerous" at number one and changed what major-label rock sounded like for the rest of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 24, 1991 — Nirvana, Kurt Cobain, Krist Novoselic, Dave Grohl. The lead single was "Smells Like Teen Spirit." The infant on the cover, Spencer Elden, later sued the band (unsuccessfully) for using his image.

events.title: Emancipation Proclamation Takes Effect
events.blurb: President Abraham Lincoln's executive order declaring freedom for all enslaved people in Confederate states in active rebellion took legal effect at the new year, transforming the character of the war from a constitutional dispute over secession into an explicit struggle over slavery. The proclamation did not free enslaved people in border states still in the Union, but it authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army — eventually nearly 200,000 would serve.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1863 — Washington, D.C. Lincoln spent the morning shaking hundreds of hands at a White House reception; by the time he sat down to sign the Proclamation his hand trembled so badly he paused. "If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act," he said.

events.title: Little Rock Nine
events.blurb: Nine Black teenagers, escorted by federal troops, walked through the front doors of an Arkansas capital's previously all-white high school, three weeks after the governor had called out the National Guard to bar them. The images of the 101st Airborne at the schoolhouse door — bayonets fixed — broadcast on the nightly news forced a hostile public to confront massive resistance.
events.revealBlurb: September 25, 1957 — Central High School, Little Rock. President Eisenhower federalized the entire Arkansas National Guard to override Governor Orval Faubus. One of the nine, Elizabeth Eckford, was famously photographed walking alone through a screaming mob on an earlier attempt.

events.title: Greensboro Sit-Ins
events.blurb: Four Black college freshmen sat down at the segregated lunch counter of a downtown variety store in a North Carolina city and politely ordered coffee. When refused service, they stayed seated until closing. They returned the next day with more students. Within two months, similar sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states, and the variety-store chain desegregated its counters.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 1960 — Woolworth's lunch counter, Greensboro. The original four were students at North Carolina A&T State University: Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil, David Richmond. Part of the counter is now in the Smithsonian.

events.title: James Meredith at Ole Miss
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Air Force veteran, after a year of legal battles, became the first Black student to enroll at a Mississippi university with a deep segregationist tradition. His arrival on campus sparked a night-long riot by a mob of 3,000 whites that killed two people and injured hundreds. Federal marshals and troops protected him through graduation.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1962 — Oxford, Mississippi. President Kennedy sent 30,000 federal troops, the largest domestic military deployment since the Civil War. Governor Ross Barnett had personally tried to block Meredith four times. Meredith graduated with a degree in political science.

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: Doom Uploaded to the Internet
events.blurb: At midnight, id Software attempted to upload its new game to a university FTP server. So many people were already waiting that the network collapsed. When the file finally went live, 10,000 simultaneous downloads crashed it again. Doom popularised the first-person shooter genre, the shareware distribution model, online multiplayer, user-generated mods, and the moral panic about video game violence — all within a few months.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1993 — id Software uploaded Doom to an FTP server at the University of Wisconsin–Madison after working 30 consecutive hours. The game sold over 2 million retail copies and was installed on an estimated 10 million PCs via shareware by 1995.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: Minecraft Officially Released
events.blurb: A game with no story, no tutorial, no win state, and graphics that looked like 1989 asked players to punch trees and build whatever they wanted. It became the best-selling video game of all time. Schools adopted it as an educational tool. A generation learned their first lessons about architecture, resource management, and server administration inside it.
events.revealBlurb: November 18, 2011 — Minecraft version 1.0.0 launched at Minecon in Las Vegas. Microsoft acquired developer Mojang in 2014 for $2.5 billion. By 2025 the game had sold over 350 million copies — more than twice the second-best-selling game.

events.title: Fortnite Battle Royale Mode Launches
events.blurb: Epic released a free-to-play mode in which 100 players parachuted onto an island and fought until one survived, funded entirely by cosmetic purchases. Within two months it had more players than any game in history. It didn't invent the battle royale genre, but it perfected the business model — and convinced the rest of the industry that free-to-play with optional cosmetics was the future.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2017 — Fortnite Battle Royale launched free on PC, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One. Within two months it had 45 million players. The game's in-game concerts — including Travis Scott's 2020 event with 12.3 million simultaneous viewers — redefined live entertainment.

events.title: Jenner's First Vaccination
events.blurb: A 47-year-old English country doctor in Gloucestershire inoculated an 8-year-old boy with pus scraped from the hand of a milkmaid who had contracted cowpox, a mild disease related to smallpox but harmless in humans. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with actual smallpox. The boy did not get sick. The doctor wrote up his results, which transformed public health across the world over the next two centuries.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1796 — Edward Jenner inoculated James Phipps. The word "vaccine" comes from vacca (Latin for cow). Jenner refused to patent the procedure despite the enormous potential fortune, insisting it was a gift to humanity. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only disease eliminated through vaccination.

events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: Salk Polio Vaccine
events.blurb: The University of Michigan School of Public Health announced that the 40-year-old Pittsburgh virologist's killed-virus polio vaccine — tested the previous year on 1.8 million children in the largest medical trial then conducted — was "safe, effective, and potent." Polio, which had paralyzed 57,000 American children in 1952, became a preventable disease overnight. Millions wept in the streets. The vaccine's developer was offered a patent; he famously refused.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1955 — Jonas Salk. Edward R. Murrow asked him who owned the patent; he answered: "Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?" The Sabin oral vaccine, using live attenuated virus, arrived 1961 and became the standard globally.

events.title: First CT Scanner
events.blurb: A British engineer at a small electronics company introduced the first clinical computed tomography scanner, which used X-ray beams and computer reconstruction to produce cross-sectional images of the inside of a patient — the first medical imaging breakthrough since the X-ray 76 years earlier. Early scans took hours and resolved only the head; within a decade the technology could produce full-body scans in minutes.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1971 — Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI; first clinical scan at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, Wimbledon, London. Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel with Allan Cormack. EMI funded the research from its Beatles albums revenue.

events.title: Munich Agreement
events.blurb: Four heads of government met through the night in a grand hall in southern Europe and handed over a democratic nation's border region to an aggressive neighbour — without inviting a single representative of that nation to the table. The leader who returned home waving the signed paper declared it meant peace; within six months the entire country had been swallowed.
events.revealBlurb: September 30, 1938 — Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler, and Mussolini signed over the Sudetenland at 1:30 AM. Chamberlain's "peace for our time" paper became history's most mocked diplomatic document. Czechoslovakia's envoys waited in an anteroom and were simply informed of the result.

events.title: Enigma Broken at Bletchley
events.blurb: A team of mathematicians and linguists working in a cluttered hut in the English countryside deployed an electromechanical machine that could test thousands of rotor settings per minute, cracking the daily-changed cipher used by an opposing military's command and logistics networks — and began reading intercepted messages within hours of their transmission.
events.revealBlurb: May 1940 — Bletchley Park's upgraded Bombe, designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, began breaking Luftwaffe "Red" traffic daily. The secret was so tightly held that some commanders were fed cover stories about lucky reconnaissance flights. The intelligence was codenamed Ultra and arguably shortened the conflict by two years.

events.title: Battle of Crete
events.blurb: For the first time in military history, an entire island was invaded and captured primarily by paratroopers and glider-borne troops alone, dropped onto an enemy-held coastline in the face of fierce resistance. The attackers suffered such catastrophic losses on the opening day that the tactic was never repeated at this scale.
events.revealBlurb: May 20 – June 1, 1941 — Operation Mercury. German paratroopers suffered over 6,500 casualties, including roughly 3,000 killed. Hitler was so shaken he banned future mass airborne operations. The British, Australian, and New Zealand defenders were evacuated; 5,000 were left behind and taken prisoner.

events.title: Death of Hitler
events.blurb: The dictator who had triggered the continent's most destructive conflict, directed the murder of millions, and sworn never to be taken alive shot himself in a subterranean command centre beneath a capital city now surrounded by enemy armies, having married his companion the previous day and designated a naval admiral as his successor.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1945 — Hitler shot himself at approximately 3:30 PM in the Führerbunker; Eva Braun took cyanide. Their bodies were carried to the garden and burned. By explicit prior order, no intact corpse was to fall into enemy hands. Soviet forces found the remains eight days after the surrender; Stalin kept the truth of their forensic identification secret for decades.

events.title: Nuremberg Verdicts
events.blurb: An international tribunal delivered verdicts against 22 senior leaders of a defeated regime after ten months of proceedings that introduced "crimes against humanity" as a concept in international law — finding twelve guilty of offences for which they would be executed, and establishing the principle that following government orders is not a defence against such charges.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1946. Hermann Göring cheated the hangman by swallowing a cyanide capsule hours before his scheduled execution — a capsule no one ever satisfactorily explained. The other ten were hanged on October 16. Three defendants were acquitted. The tribunal's procedural framework became the model for every subsequent international war crimes court.

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Babe Ruth's Called Shot
events.blurb: A Yankee slugger, facing a Cubs pitcher in game 3 of a World Series at a Chicago ballpark amid heckling from the dugout and the crowd, gestured with his bat toward the center field bleachers and then, on the next pitch, hit a home run that landed roughly where he had pointed. Whether he had actually "called" the shot is debated among eyewitnesses and film analysts to this day; teammates and opponents offered contradictory accounts for decades. The legend has long since outgrown the facts.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1932 — Babe Ruth at Wrigley Field. Opposing pitcher: Charlie Root, who denied the called shot to his death. An 8mm home movie shot by a Chicago fan, discovered in 1992, shows Ruth pointing — but whether to the outfield or the Cubs dugout is still contested.

events.title: Michael Jordan's First Retirement
events.blurb: Three months after winning his third straight NBA championship and four months after his father had been murdered in a highway robbery, the 30-year-old best basketball player in the world held a press conference announcing his retirement from the game. He had "lost the desire to play," he said. Months later he was playing minor-league baseball for a Chicago White Sox affiliate. He would return to the NBA 17 months after his retirement, winning three more championships.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1993 — Michael Jordan. His AA baseball season with the Birmingham Barons ended with a .202 batting average. His return to the NBA, announced March 18, 1995 with the two-word press release "I'm back," drew him to four more championships (1996, 1997, 1998) before a second retirement, then a third comeback with the Washington Wizards.

events.title: India Wins Cricket World Cup
events.blurb: The Indian men's cricket team won their second-ever Cricket World Cup, beating Sri Lanka by six wickets in the final at a Mumbai stadium in front of a home crowd that included the country's most beloved cricketer, who was playing in his sixth and final World Cup. The tournament winner's 36-year-old captain carried the little master on his shoulders around the stadium in celebration. It was the first time any nation had won a World Cup final on its own soil.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 2011 — India beat Sri Lanka at Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai. Captain MS Dhoni hit the winning six. Sachin Tendulkar's 28 runs in his final-ever ODI innings on the way to the trophy saw him carried on teammates' shoulders around the stadium.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: Netflix Launches Streaming
events.blurb: A decade-old Silicon Valley mail-order DVD rental company launched an online video-streaming service, initially offering subscribers limited hours of instant streaming on top of their physical DVD subscriptions. The library at launch had about 1,000 titles and required Internet Explorer. The service would eventually make the DVD operation so irrelevant that the company's own name became an anachronism (net-flicks via mail).
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 2007 — initial subscribers got 1 hour of streaming per dollar paid per month. In 2011, CEO Reed Hastings attempted to split DVDs into a sister brand "Qwikster"; the backlash was so severe he reversed within three weeks.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: Snapchat Launched
events.blurb: Three Stanford undergraduates released an iOS app that let users send photos that automatically disappeared a few seconds after being viewed. One founder had pitched the idea for a product-design class the previous spring and been told it was terrible. The app would grow explosively as a teenage-first social platform and introduce "Stories," a format quickly copied by every major competitor.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2011 — Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown. Originally named Picaboo. Facebook offered to acquire Snap for $3 billion in 2013; Spiegel said no. Snap went public in 2017 at a $24 billion valuation.
